extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and readers of American journalism history; journalists interested in historical practices
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts criteria and standards implicit and explicit in a historical account of American newspapers (c.1892–1914), for evaluating newspaper quality, practices, and impact. Focuses on editorial policy, business management, presentation, ethics, and political influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modernization of newspaper operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Processes of modernizing a paper’s business and production practices (e.g., overhauling archaic advertising methods, founding a Sunday edition, erecting a new building).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example wording: 'The Sunpaper ... underwent a process of modernization beginning in 1904. The archaic advertising methods were overhauled, a Sunday edition was founded, and a new building was erected.' Modernization is linked to competitiveness and revival of prestige and circulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Front-page and editorial-page presentation conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Format choices such as keeping 'a front page clear of advertising' and devoting the last page to 'displayed editorials.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As with the Christian Science Monitor: 'A handsome ten-page paper, with a front page clear of advertising and the last page devoted to displayed editorials.' Such presentation signals editorial seriousness and distinction from purely commercial papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crime/disaster coverage policy (the Monitor taboo)
rubrics_metrics.description: A deliberate editorial policy to limit or 'play down' crime and disaster news, printing such stories only when government or society is materially affected or when benevolent response is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original phrasing: 'The Monitor printed crime stories only when government or society was materially affected, and disaster news only when it had similar importance or when it called for benevolent response — and even then it "played it down."' Anti-pattern: sensational crime coverage aimed at circulation rather than public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of foreign news and feature coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Strength and breadth of foreign reporting and cultural features (art, music, literature), and the existence of foreign bureaus and services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Its foreign news and its features ... were excellent' and 'It established bureaus in the leading American cities and foreign capitals.' High-quality foreign service expands national and international influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political stance and editorial independence
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper’s declared or de facto political alignment, willingness to break with local machines, and degree of independence in editorial policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the Sun's 'open break with the machine' and support for a Republican candidate despite Democratic tradition. Independence can increase influence but may carry risk; switching parties or positions affects reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crusading/investigative journalism as a technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of organized campaigns or crusades (investigations, exposés, editorial pressure) to influence public policy, legal action, or elections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include the Tribune/Record-Herald's Lorimer exposé and the World’s campaigns. Guidance: crusades can produce prosecutions and political outcomes ('led the United States Senate to throw William Lorimer out of that body'), but are also tied to yellow-press methods and may be used for circulation gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensationalism and 'yellow' techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of sensational content, startling typography, melodramatic stories, and emotional human-interest treatment to attract readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrased as 'yellow journalism' and illustrated by the Denver Post's red-and-black banners, 'sob-sister' stories, and buying feature material to keep it out of rivals' hands. Anti-patterns: libel suits, mob violence, ethical concerns, and damage to reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business and managerial competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability of owners and managers to run newspaper enterprises profitably and sustainably (investing/reinvesting capital, competent business decisions, avoiding over-leverage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Munsey 'generally a failure as a newspaper manager'; Kohlsaat paying too much and having to turn over properties; Hearst discontinuing editions. Good management affects long-term survival and editorial capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation strategy and number of daily editions
rubrics_metrics.description: Practices concerning how many editions are published (multiple daily editions, morning/evening variants), and strategies to grow circulation (Sunday editions, expanded distribution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Daily News 'published half a dozen editions daily'; Tribune claimed the largest morning circulation. Edition strategy interacts with advertising and content planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of illustrations, advertising reliance, and promotional pricing
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which a paper relies on illustrations, heavy advertising, coupon and pricing schemes, and subscription promotions to increase readership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the Daily News 'used much illustration... and carried heavy advertising' and Kohlsaat's 'effective circulation promoter by the use of various coupon schemes.' Premium wars (e.g., free gasoline with want-ads) are extreme promotional tactics with financial risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotional stunts and sponsored adventures
rubrics_metrics.description: Sponsoring high-profile stunts or expeditions (e.g., polar attempts, dirigible flights) as publicity and feature content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Walter Wellman's North Pole and transatlantic dirigible attempts sponsored by the Record-Herald. Stunts can raise profile but are risky and may fail or draw ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics and conflicts of interest (payments, blackmail allegations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance of 'good will' payments, paid influence by private interests, alleged blackmail of advertisers, and other ethical compromises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: papers accepting monthly 'good will' payments from Southern Pacific; accusations (never legally proven) that Bonfils blackmailed advertisers; Committee on Ethics recommending expulsion. Ethical lapses threaten credibility and may provoke institutional sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial leadership and personality-driven direction
rubrics_metrics.description: Impact of an editor’s character, convictions, and leadership on a paper’s tone, crusading zeal, and editorial choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Grasty's 'pugnacious' crusading, Older as a dominating crusader organizing prosecutions, Keeley filling front pages with victims’ names. Strong personalities can drive reforms or excesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printing and overall presentation quality
rubrics_metrics.description: General quality of printing, layout, and aesthetic presentation as markers of seriousness versus sensationalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrase: 'papers were generally well printed, less sensational than those of New York.' Good printing and tasteful layout support credibility and reader trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic reach and distribution strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a paper is primarily local/regional or has wider national/international distribution (and the implications for influence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Monitor's circulation 'distributed more generally over the United States than that of any other daily' and notable foreign circulation. Broader distribution increases political and cultural influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of syndicates to control feature material
rubrics_metrics.description: Purchasing or hoarding syndicate material to strengthen one's paper and deny content to rivals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted: papers 'buying most of what was offered in order to keep it out of the hands of rivals but using only the best of the articles, columns, pictures, and comic strips of the syndicates.' This is a competitive tactic with implications for content uniqueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mission orientation: paternalism and advocacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-assigned roles such as acting as a regional 'guardian' or paternalistic advocate for a territory or set of reforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the Post calling itself 'Your Big Brother' and 'The Paper with a Heart and Soul,' appointing itself guardian of Colorado, Wyoming, and New Mexico. Such missions shape editorial priorities and crusades; they can benefit publics but also be self-serving.
